title: Friends in good times
hook: everyone is a companion in pleasure; in trouble, few remain (Sorath M9, ang 634)

segments.voice: Yesterday, unmoved by pain, and your line: level in all weather. Did you catch yourself adding the second pain? Today the ninth Guru looks at the people around us when the weather turns. Day five hundred eighty-three.
screen: `UNMOVED BY PAIN — LEVEL IN ALL WEATHER.`

segments.voice: When someone gets a promotion, the group chat lights up. Congratulations, drinks on you, so proud of you, a row of party emojis. When the same person loses the job six months later, the chat goes quiet. A couple of people send a private message. Most say nothing, not out of cruelty, but because they don't know what to say, and it's easier to look away. Guru Tegh Bahadur saw it too, long before group chats, and put it in a hymn.
screen: `A PROMOTION: THE CHAT LIGHTS UP.` → `A LOSS: THE CHAT GOES QUIET.` → `HE SAW IT TOO.`

segments.voice: The hymn in Raag Sorath begins, in paraphrase: friend, understand this in your mind. The world is bound up in its own comfort; no one truly belongs to anyone. Then the picture. In good times, many come and sit with you, crowding round on every side. When trouble falls, they all leave your company, and no one comes near. Sukh is comfort, good times. Bipat is trouble, calamity. The hymn's line runs between those two words. Then it goes further than most of us would dare. Even the one at home who loved you most, it says, when the soul leaves the body, runs away crying ghost. It's a hard sentence, and it's meant to be. The point isn't that people are wicked. It's that human love, left to itself, is tangled up with what we get from each other. The hymn ends: at the last, says Nanak, nothing helps except the Lord. Now look at today's practice, because it turns the hymn around. The hymn describes the world's way. It doesn't tell you to become bitter about it. If everyone drifts off when trouble comes, then the one who stays is rare, and the Sikh tradition prizes that rarity. Look at the sangat that turns up with food when someone dies, sitting with the family for days while the Guru Granth Sahib is read. That's a whole community built to stay. The hymn describes how the world tends to drift away. The practice asks you to be the exception. Stay in hard times.
screen: `NO ONE TRULY BELONGS TO ANYONE.` · `SUKH: MANY COME AND SIT.` · `BIPAT: NO ONE COMES NEAR.` · `BE THE ONE WHO STAYS.` · then, large: `STAY IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with someone in trouble. Sit quietly and let one name come to mind, someone going through something hard right now. Illness, a breakup, a job lost, a long grief. Picture them clearly. Notice if part of you has been keeping away, not sure what to say. Then decide one way to come near: a message, a visit, a meal left at the door, a call where you mostly listen. You don't need wise words. You need to show up. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Friends in good times. Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymn says many sit with us in sukh, good times, and few come near in bipat, trouble.
Your line: stay in hard times. Today, send the message to the person in trouble, the one you've been putting off. Two lines is enough. Day five hundred eighty-three.

screen: `DAY 583 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY SEARCH IN THE FOREST.`

howItsDone: When a Sikh family loses someone, the sangat often gathers at the home with food and support while a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is held, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns and saloks are commonly heard at that time.

myth: the hymn tells us to become bitter about friends
it describes the world's way; the practice asks you to be the one who stays.
the hymn says the world is bound up in its own comfort
no one truly belongs to anyone, it says.
the hymn says even the closest ones run away when the soul leaves the body
it's a hard line, meant to show how tangled human love is.

fork.setup: in the Sorath hymn, trouble falls on someone who had many friends. what do the friends do?
options: leave, and no one comes near.
fork.reveal: in good times many sit round on every side; when trouble falls, they all leave, and no one comes near. at the last, says Nanak, only the Lord helps.

original.note: Gurmukhi: preet, love. The hymn looks honestly at how much of our preet is tied to our own comfort.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hymn is cynical about friendship.
what it means: it tells the truth about how love clings to comfort, so we can rest in the Lord and become the friend who stays.
what a scholar hears: the soul in the hymn is called hans, the swan, an old image in Indian poetry for the spirit that flies off when the body dies.

sources.ref: Raag Sorath, Mahalla 9, 'preetam jaan lehu man maahee' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 634)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the 'three and a half centuries' date and the sweeping 'almost everyone' and 'how most friendships end'; stock 'Think of' reworded.

Paraphrase of the shabad (preetam jaan lehu man maahee; apne sukh sio hee jag phaandhio ko kaahoo ko naahee; sukh mai aan bahut mil baithat rahat chahoo dis gherai; bipat paree sabh hee sang chhaadit ko-oo na aavat nerai; ghar kee naar ... jab hee hans tajee ih kaaneiaa pret pret kar bhaagee; ... ant baar naanak bin har jee ko-oo kaam na aaio): please confirm wording and Ang 634.
The line about the wife fleeing crying 'ghost' is softened to 'the one at home who loved you most'; a Keeper may want to handle it differently.
Description of the sangat's support after a death is general practice; please confirm.
